chunks: Keeping ground variation small. The question: How do you avoid too much variation?
To keep ground voltage differences small, you attack from two sides.
Make the ground path low in resistance and inductance: a solid plane close to the signals, no slots or narrow necks, and plenty of vias.
And make the currents in shared ground paths small and local: decoupling capacitors at the pins, tiny switching loops and slower edges.
Keep noisy and quiet circuits apart, and check with probe points.
Think of quieting a noisy street. You can widen the road so traffic flows easily: that is lowering the ground's resistance and inductance.
You can cut the number of cars and their speed: that is lowering the current and how fast it changes. Sending trucks away from the school is partitioning.
A sound meter outside the school is the probe point. The analogy is loose: ground has no "street" of its own, only the copper you give it.
A typical four-layer stackup keeps a continuous ground plane just 0. 1-0. 2 mm below the top signal layer.
The tiny gap makes the signal-return loop thin, so its inductance per square is only a fraction of a nanohenry. Compare with a 1-nH-per-mm trace with no nearby plane.
Inductance: resistance to sudden changes in current, in nanohenries (nH). It makes a voltage L di over dt .
Decoupling capacitor: a nearby capacitor that supplies fast current so it does not flow through the plane ("Placing and routing decoupling capacitors").
Ground bounce: a ground shift when many outputs switch together. ADC and LSB: a chip that turns a voltage into a number, and its smallest step.
Error budget: the allowed ground shift, from which you work backward to milliohms and nanohenries.
A 12-bit, 3. 3 volts ADC has steps of about 0. 81 millivolts, so half a step is about 0. 4 millivolts.
If 100 milliamps of return current crosses a shared path, its resistance must be under 0. 4 millivolts / 0. 1 amps = 4 milliohms, about 8 square patches of standard copper at 0.
49 milliohms each. For ground bounce, say 8 outputs each switch 20 milliamps in 1 nanoseconds, and the shift must stay under 100 millivolts.
Then the shared inductance must be at most 0. 1 volts over (8 times 20 milliamps over ns ) equals 0. 625 nanohenries. That is the whole idea.
"I keep ground variation small by lowering the impedance and shrinking the currents.
Impedance: a solid unbroken plane right under the signal layers, no slots or neck-downs, stitching vias at layer changes, and many ground pins on connectors.
Currents: tight decoupling at every power pin, compact switching loops, slower edges and fewer simultaneous switches.
Then I partition by placement so noisy returns stay away from sensitive analog, and I budget the allowed millivolts back to milliohms and nanohenries."
